newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower on fund selling, Fed fears.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower on fund selling, Fed fears.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended moderately weaker on Tuesday, amid a continuation of hedge fund selling and renewed fears the Federal Reserve will raise rates again in July.
The 30-year bond closed above the 7.0 percent level for the first time in a month, ending the day at 7.03 percent. Its price fell a 1/2-point to 94-31/32.
"Enough people think the Fed will go in July that the market is defensive," said Joe LaVorgna, financial market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
After the Fed opted to leave rates alone at its policy-setting meeting last week, some players figured the Fed may want to wait a bit more before tightening again.
But a record high in the Conference Board's consumer confidence index in May threw that theory out the window for now, leading many to believe the strong confidence will keep demand at high levels.
The index rose to 127.1 in May, well above April's 118.5 reading and its highest in 28 years.
"It blew people out of the water," said a head trader at a U.S. primary dealership. "Nobody was ready for that."
The trader noted that consumer confidence typically is not a huge market mover. "But it was the magnitude of the number that caught people off guard," he said.
Treasury prices were already heading south before the data, as traders reported heavy selling by large hedge funds in longer-dated, non-active issues, which spilled over into active issues.
Some said funds continued to unwind so-called yen carry trades, which began a couple weeks ago when the dollar first started to slide.
Yet, some market participants noted that Treasuries would have fallen further if not for a recovery in the dollar up to 116.68 yen and 1.7067 marks.

Also, the market was further supported late in the session by a weaker-than-expected sales report. Redbook Research reported a 0.5-percent rise in sales the week ended May 24, below the 0.8-percent gain in the prior week.

With many traders taking an extended holiday weekend following the day off on Monday for Memorial Day, volume was on the light side. Volume was about $70 billion by 1600 EDT/2000 GMT, according to GovPX.
Activity looks to pick up on Wednesday, but players do not expect a different result from Tuesday.

Kicking off the session will be the Commerce Department's durable goods report for April. Economists polled by Reuters forecast a 1.3 percent rise. But analysts conceded that durable goods were difficult to predict, adding that the report was subject to large swings and revisions.
Economists said data could come in on the weak side, weighed down by various strikes at auto production plants.
"If durables are weak, you could gain back the five basis points (in yield) you lost today," LaVorgna said.

Durable goods, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, will likely be the catalyst to trading early in the session, before the market turns its attention to the Treasury's $16.5 billion two-year note auction at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.

The when-issued two-year note ended Tuesday's session at 6.31 percent, but further concessions may still be needed, some experts said. "We could back up another two, three basis points," said Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities.
Analysts said the issue was still too expensive if the Fed raised rates in July.
The Treasury will also sell $12.0 billion five-year notes on Thursday. The when-issued five-year note finished at 6.63 percent.
In late trading, the oustanding two-year note was down 2/32 to 100-6/32 to yield 6.27 percent, while the five-year note was at at 100-2/32, down 6/32, to yield 6.62 percent.
The 10-year note was down 10/32 to 98-26/32 to yield 6.79, and T-bill rates were unchanged to one basis point higher.
